name: Headquarters Position
description: Master Headquarters Position in BJJ - the central hub for systematic guard passing. Learn control mechanics, multiple passing pathways, defensive escapes, and achieve 70% advancement rate with this strategic position.
variant_uniqueness: Systematic passing hub with versatile control
overview:
**Headquarters Position** in BJJ is a guard passing control position where you control one of your opponent's legs while maintaining an upright posture and wide base. It serves as the central hub for modern systematic guard passing, allowing you to choose from multiple passing options (**[[Knee Slice Pass]]**, **[[Long Step Pass]]**, **[[Smash Pass]]**) based on your opponent's defensive reactions. This position offers low-risk, high-control passing with 70% advancement rate for beginners and 95% for advanced practitioners.

**Headquarters** (also called Headquarters Control) acts as a strategic decision point in guard passing systems. The position creates exceptional control with relatively low risk, limiting the bottom player's defensive options while maintaining multiple offensive pathways. From **[[Combat Base]]** or **[[Half Guard]]** top positions, you establish leg control that compresses infinite guard passing complexity into finite if-then decision sequences.

The position's effectiveness stems from controlling one opponent leg between your legs with downward knee pressure, posting your support leg wide for triangulated base, and maintaining upright posture that prevents sweeps. You can flow seamlessly between **[[Knee Slice Pass]]**, **[[Long Step Pass]]**, **[[Smash Pass]]**, and **[[Leg Weave Pass]]** variations, making this one of the most versatile positions in contemporary guard passing systems.

This position represents a fundamental evolution in guard passing theory popularized by John Danaher's systematic passing methodology. It moves away from commitment-heavy explosive passes toward measured, reactive approaches that maintain safety while threatening multiple directions simultaneously. The passer can probe defenses methodically, returning to headquarters between attempts rather than overcommitting to single directions, creating grinding systematic pressure that exhausts defensive options over time.
state_invariants: One opponent leg controlled and pinned between top player's legs with knee driven toward mat by shin or knee pressure, restricting hip mobility and preventing guard recovery through sustained downward pressure

Supporting leg firmly posted wide on mat creating stable triangular base typically positioned 45-90 degrees from controlled leg, providing stability against sweeps while allowing dynamic weight transfer for passing attacks

Upright posture maintained with spine aligned vertically and perpendicular to mat, head up with shoulders positioned over hips rather than leaning forward, creating structural integrity that prevents breakdown and maintains balance

Control hand grips opponent's knee, thigh, or pants at knee line while opposite hand controls lapel, collar, or establishes underhook, preventing frames while maintaining distance management and preventing opponent from establishing defensive structures

Opponent's hips flattened to mat or controlled through combination of leg pressure and upper body control, limiting mobility and ability to create hip movement necessary for guard retention or sweep attempts
prerequisites: Solid understanding of base mechanics and weight distribution principles in top positions
Ability to establish and maintain knee-line control against resistance from various guard configurations
Familiarity with fundamental guard passing concepts, timing, and systematic passing methodology
Recognition of opponent's defensive patterns, guard retention strategies, and common escape sequences
Competence in grip fighting and hand positioning to establish initial control from standing or combat base
key_principles: Control opponent's leg by driving knee firmly toward mat, eliminating their ability to create frames or recover guard structure through sustained pressure
Establish strong posting base with opposite leg positioned wide and perpendicular to opponent's body line, creating triangular structure resistant to sweeps
Maintain upright posture with strong spine alignment and vertical orientation, preventing forward weight shift that creates rolling opportunities or compromises balance
Create and manipulate passing angles by adjusting hip position and weight distribution while maintaining connection with trapped leg throughout transitions
Control opponent's hip mobility through strategic placement of trapped leg and systematic pressure application that limits their movement options
Neutralize opponent's frames and hooks by maintaining distance with posting hand while controlling with gripping hand, preventing them from creating space
Systematically eliminate defensive options by reading reactions and selecting appropriate passing variations, using headquarters as central decision hub

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to create frames and space with hands or feet to prevent passing pressure
Opponent turns toward trapped leg attempting to recover half guard structure or full guard
Opponent extends leg to create distance or pushes knee line with foot on hip
Opponent commits to deep half guard entry or underhook attack creating back exposure

decision_tree.condition: If opponent keeps leg straight and attempts to push knee line with foot on hip creating distance
If opponent turns toward trapped leg attempting to recover half guard or full guard structures
If opponent creates strong frames with hands on shoulder and hip attempting to maintain distance
If opponent attempts deep half guard entry or commits to underhook sweep mechanics

common_errors.error: Poor knee control with insufficient pressure on opponent's knee line
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to recover guard structure, create effective frames, or enter into half guard positions that neutralize passing momentum and reset position to opponent's advantage
common_errors.correction: Drive knee firmly toward mat using weight from hips, pinning opponent's knee and restricting hip mobility through constant downward pressure maintained throughout entire passing sequence

common_errors.error: Excessive forward lean with weight shifted over hands rather than hips and chest
common_errors.consequence: Creates vulnerability to forward rolls, off-balancing sweeps, and granby roll escapes while compromising base stability and reaction time to opponent movements
common_errors.correction: Keep spine upright and perpendicular to mat, distributing weight through hips and posting leg while using hands for balance and control rather than weight support

common_errors.error: Insufficient base width with posting leg positioned too close to opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Reduces stability against lateral sweeps and makes passer vulnerable to being pushed or pulled off balance during opponent's escape attempts or sweep mechanics
common_errors.correction: Post supporting leg wide and away from opponent's centerline creating triangular base with posting foot angled perpendicular to opponent's body for maximum stability

common_errors.error: Passive positioning without active pressure or advancing intention
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent time to develop escape sequences, recover guard structures, or create effective defensive frames that prevent progression and eliminate passing advantages
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant forward pressure while reading opponent's reactions, continuously threatening multiple passing options to prevent opponent from settling into defensive patterns

common_errors.error: Telegraphing pass direction through premature weight shifts or grip changes
common_errors.consequence: Opponent anticipates passing direction and establishes defensive structures or escape routes before passer can complete technique, neutralizing passing attempts
common_errors.correction: Maintain neutral position until opponent commits to defensive pattern, then explosively execute appropriate counter-pass while using feints and subtle adjustments to disguise intentions

common_errors.error: Losing connection with trapped leg during transitional moments between passes
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers full guard or creates scramble situations that eliminate passing advantages and reset position to neutral or worse positions
common_errors.correction: Maintain leg control throughout entire passing sequence using consistent pressure, ensuring new control is established before releasing original grip during transitions

training_drills.name: Headquarters Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts in headquarters with one leg trapped. Bottom player uses various escape attempts including frames, shrimps, deep half entries, and guard recovery while top player maintains position and adjusts base. Focus on weight distribution, posting mechanics, and knee control pressure throughout opponent's defensive movements.
training_drills.duration: 3 minutes per round, 3-4 rounds per partner

training_drills.name: Headquarters Passing Cycle
training_drills.description: From established headquarters position, cycle through all primary passing options including knee slice, long step, smash pass, and leg weave based on coach's calls or timer intervals. Bottom player provides progressive resistance. Emphasizes reading reactions and selecting appropriate passing variations while maintaining headquarters as central hub.
training_drills.duration: 5 minutes continuous flow, 2-3 rounds per partner

training_drills.name: Recovery to Headquarters Drill
training_drills.description: Start from compromised positions where opponent has frames, partial guard recovery, or defensive grips established. Work to re-establish headquarters control against resistance. Develops ability to find and maintain headquarters position during live rolling and competition scenarios with realistic resistance levels.
training_drills.duration: 2 minutes per scenario, 5-6 different starting positions

how_to_establish_headquarters.question: How Do You Establish Headquarters Position in BJJ?
how_to_establish_headquarters.answer: Follow these 12 steps to establish and maintain **Headquarters Position** from **[[Half Guard]]** or **[[Combat Base]]**:

steps.action: Start from Combat Base or standing position facing opponent's guard
steps.detail: Begin with proper posture: spine vertical, weight distributed through hips and feet, hands ready for grip engagement

steps.action: Control opponent's near leg at the knee line
steps.detail: Grip opponent's knee or pants at knee level with your lead hand, establishing initial leg control point

steps.action: Drive your shin or knee into opponent's trapped thigh
steps.detail: Position your lead leg's shin or knee against opponent's thigh, applying downward pressure toward the mat to pin the leg

steps.action: Post your support leg wide at 45-90 degree angle
steps.detail: Place your opposite foot firmly on mat positioned wide from opponent's body, creating stable triangular base structure

steps.action: Maintain upright posture with vertical spine
steps.detail: Keep your torso perpendicular to mat, head up, shoulders aligned over hips - do not lean forward excessively
Your free hand controls opponent's collar, lapel, or establishes underhook while maintaining distance management

steps.action: Drive constant downward pressure through trapped leg
steps.detail: Use hip weight to pin opponent's knee toward mat, eliminating their ability to create frames or recover guard

steps.action: Flatten opponent's hips to the mat
steps.detail: Combine leg pressure with upper body control to prevent hip elevation and restrict opponent's mobility

steps.action: Adjust base angle based on opponent reactions
steps.detail: Shift posting foot position and hip angle to counter opponent's escape attempts while maintaining connection
Control distance with posting hand on hip or chest, preventing opponent from establishing effective pushing frames
Observe whether opponent extends leg (signals long step), turns toward you (signals knee slice), or creates frames (signals smash pass)

steps.action: Select and execute appropriate passing variation
steps.detail: Based on opponent's reaction, flow into **[[Knee Slice Pass]]**, **[[Long Step Pass]]**, **[[Smash Pass]]**, or **[[Leg Weave Pass]]**

when_to_use_headquarters.question: When Should You Use Headquarters Position?
when_to_use_headquarters.answer: **Headquarters Position** excels in specific strategic scenarios:

scenarios.situation: Against various guard types requiring systematic breakdown
scenarios.explanation: Use headquarters when facing **[[Closed Guard]]**, **[[Half Guard]]**, **[[Butterfly Guard]]**, or **[[Open Guard]]** configurations that require methodical passing rather than explosive techniques. The position provides stable control platform for reading and countering defensive patterns.

scenarios.situation: When you need low-risk passing with high control
scenarios.explanation: Choose headquarters over explosive passes when energy conservation matters, when facing dangerous guard players, or in competition scenarios where point position matters more than submission attempts. The low energy cost (Low) and high time sustainability (Long) make it ideal for grinding pressure.

scenarios.situation: After breaking closed guard or recovering from failed pass attempt
scenarios.explanation: Headquarters serves as recovery position after **[[Guard Opening Sequence]]** or when your initial passing attempt gets partially defended. Return to headquarters to reset and select better passing angle based on new defensive information.

scenarios.situation: Against opponents with strong sweep game from guard
scenarios.explanation: The triangulated base structure and upright posture make headquarters highly resistant to sweeps compared to forward-pressure passing styles. Use it when opponent has demonstrated effective **[[Butterfly Sweep]]**, **[[Scissor Sweep]]**, or **[[Hip Bump Sweep]]** capabilities.

scenarios.situation: When learning systematic guard passing methodology
scenarios.explanation: Beginners and intermediates benefit from headquarters' clear decision tree structure. The if-then passing sequences (extend leg → long step, turn toward you → knee slice, create frames → smash) simplify complex passing scenarios into manageable choices.

defensive_perspective.question: How Do You Escape Headquarters Position from Bottom?
defensive_perspective.answer: From bottom in **Headquarters Position**, your defensive priorities include creating space, recovering guard structures, and preventing passing advancement:

escape_mechanics.technique: Frame and Shrimp to Half Guard
escape_mechanics.execution: Establish strong frames with hands on opponent's shoulder and hip, execute shrimp movement to create space, recover your trapped leg to **[[Half Guard]]** structure. Focus on preventing knee slice direction by turning toward trapped leg. (Success Rate: 45%)
escape_mechanics.key_detail: Push on hip to prevent opponent's forward pressure while simultaneously pulling trapped leg back using hip movement

escape_mechanics.execution: Create initial space with frames, post your free hand behind you, drive off posting hand while bringing free leg between you and opponent to **[[Technical Standup]]** position. Requires timing when opponent shifts weight forward. (Success Rate: 30%)
escape_mechanics.key_detail: Execute explosively when opponent commits weight to passing attempt, capitalizing on their momentary loss of base

escape_mechanics.execution: As opponent drives forward for pass, dive underneath with shoulder and arm, recovering your trapped leg to **[[Deep Half Guard]]** position. This works especially well against smash pass or leg weave attempts. (Success Rate: 35%)
escape_mechanics.key_detail: Requires perfect timing - enter as opponent commits to passing pressure, not while they maintain static headquarters control

escape_mechanics.execution: Fight for underhook on opponent's posted leg side, use underhook to off-balance opponent forward while recovering guard structure. Can lead to **[[Scramble Position]]** or guard recovery. (Success Rate: 35%)
escape_mechanics.key_detail: Combine underhook with hip escape movement to disrupt opponent's base before they establish heavy passing pressure

position_comparison.question: How Does Headquarters Compare to Other Passing Positions?

comparisons.relationship: **[[Combat Base]]** is the preceding position used to establish headquarters control. Combat base offers more mobility but less control; headquarters offers more control but requires leg commitment.
comparisons.when_to_use_each: Use combat base for initial guard approach and grip fighting. Transition to headquarters once you've isolated one leg and need stable passing platform.

comparisons.position: Knee Slice Pass (the position, not technique)
comparisons.relationship: **[[Knee Slice Pass]]** is a dynamic passing technique executed from headquarters. Headquarters is the static control position; knee slice is the movement phase.
comparisons.when_to_use_each: Establish headquarters first for control and decision-making. Execute knee slice when opponent turns toward trapped leg, committing to that specific passing direction.

comparisons.relationship: **[[Pressure Passing]]** styles use forward pressure and weight to pass. Headquarters maintains upright posture with less forward commitment but more systematic decision-making.
comparisons.when_to_use_each: Use headquarters for systematic, low-risk passing with clear decision trees. Use pressure passing when you have significant size/weight advantage or opponent has weak frames.

history_and_origins.question: Who Developed Headquarters Position?
history_and_origins.answer: **Headquarters Position** was popularized by John Danaher and his systematic guard passing methodology. Danaher's approach to Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu emphasizes treating guard passing as a systematic science rather than athletic scrambling. The headquarters concept emerged as the central hub of his passing system, taught extensively to the Danaher Death Squad (Gordon Ryan, Garry Tonon, Eddie Cummings, and others) and disseminated through his instructional series.
history_and_origins.evolution: This position represents modern evolution in guard passing theory, moving away from commitment-heavy explosive passes (common in 1990s-2000s BJJ) toward measured, reactive approaches that maintain safety while threatening multiple directions. The name 'headquarters' reflects its role as the command center or decision point from which all systematic passing routes emerge. The position gained prominence in high-level competition through Gordon Ryan's dominant performances, where his ability to maintain headquarters control while methodically selecting optimal passes demonstrated the position's effectiveness against world-class guard players.
history_and_origins.influence: The headquarters framework has influenced how guard passing is taught across BJJ, shifting instructional focus from individual passing techniques toward systematic position-based passing with clear decision trees.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is headquarters position in BJJ?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: **Headquarters Position** is a guard passing control position where you control one opponent leg between your legs while maintaining upright posture and wide base. It serves as the central hub for systematic guard passing, allowing you to choose from multiple passing options based on opponent's reactions. Success rate ranges from 70% (beginners) to 95% (advanced).

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do you do headquarters position in BJJ?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: To establish headquarters: (1) control opponent's leg at knee line, (2) drive your shin/knee into their thigh toward mat, (3) post support leg wide at 45-90 degrees, (4) maintain upright posture, (5) control opponent's upper body with grips, (6) apply constant downward pressure through trapped leg. See detailed 12-step execution sequence above.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What passes can you do from headquarters position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: From headquarters you can execute: **[[Knee Slice Pass]]** (when opponent turns toward trapped leg), **[[Long Step Pass]]** (when opponent extends leg), **[[Smash Pass]]** (when opponent creates frames), **[[Leg Weave Pass]]**, **[[Over-Under Pass]]**, **[[Underhook Pass]]**, and **[[Crossface Pass]]**. The position allows seamless flow between these options based on defensive reactions.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I use headquarters position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Use headquarters when you need systematic guard passing with low risk, when facing various guard configurations requiring methodical breakdown, after breaking **[[Closed Guard]]**, when energy conservation matters, or against opponents with strong sweep games. It's ideal for competition scenarios prioritizing position over explosive passing.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why is it called headquarters position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: It's called 'headquarters' because it serves as the central command hub of systematic guard passing methodology. Like a military headquarters where strategic decisions are made, this position is where the passer makes decisions about which passing route to select based on opponent reactions. The name emphasizes its role as a decision point rather than a committed technique.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do you escape headquarters position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Escape headquarters from bottom by: creating frames on shoulder and hip, shrimping to recover **[[Half Guard]]** (45% success), attempting **[[Technical Standup]]** (30% success), entering **[[Deep Half Guard]]** (35% success), or fighting for underhook to create scrambles (35% success). Prevent knee slice by turning toward trapped leg.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between headquarters and knee slice?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: **Headquarters** is a static control position and decision point. **[[Knee Slice Pass]]** is a dynamic passing technique executed from headquarters. Headquarters is where you control the leg and read reactions; knee slice is the movement you perform when opponent turns toward trapped leg. One is position, the other is technique.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What mistakes do beginners make in headquarters position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Common beginner mistakes: poor knee control with insufficient downward pressure (allows guard recovery), excessive forward lean (creates sweep vulnerability), insufficient base width (reduces stability), passive positioning without active pressure (gives opponent time to escape), telegraphing pass direction prematurely (opponent defends easily), losing connection during transitions (allows full guard recovery).

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is headquarters position good for beginners?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, **Headquarters Position** is excellent for beginners. It provides systematic guard passing structure with low risk (70% retention rate for beginners), multiple offensive options, and clear decision-making framework (if opponent does X, you do Y) that simplifies guard passing complexity. The upright posture and wide base also make it inherently stable against sweeps, building confidence while learning.

expert_insights.danaher: Headquarters position represents the central hub of systematic guard passing methodology where controlling the opponent's knee-line creates the fundamental decision point in modern guard passing systems. The position's power lies not in forcing any specific pass, but in creating a control structure that systematically limits the opponent's defensive options while maintaining multiple offensive pathways simultaneously. By establishing headquarters, you compress the infinite complexity of guard passing into a finite series of if-then sequences that can be executed methodically. When the opponent extends their leg, you execute long step. When they turn toward you, you execute knee slice. When they create frames, you execute smash pass. This systematic reduction transforms guard passing from a chaotic scramble into a controlled technical progression with clear decision trees. The critical principle is maintaining connection with the trapped leg throughout all transitions - this connection is the thread that ties together your entire passing system and prevents the chaos of scrambles. The biomechanical efficiency stems from the triangulated base structure combined with the mechanical advantage created by pinning the opponent's knee to the mat, which eliminates their primary tool for creating angles and recovering guard structures. Modern competitors who master headquarters can maintain this position with minimal energy expenditure while methodically breaking down even the most sophisticated guard retention systems.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, headquarters is my absolute favorite passing position because it puts maximum pressure on my opponent to make decisions while I stay relatively safe and maintain complete control of the passing sequence. When I get to headquarters, I know I'm passing - it's just a matter of which direction based on how they defend and what mistakes they make under pressure. I don't commit heavy pressure initially because I want to float just enough to make them think they can escape, which causes them to show me their defensive strategy and commit to specific movements. Once they commit to pushing my knee, turning into me, or trying to frame, I already know exactly which pass is going to work based on their defensive choice. The key is not telegraphing your intention early - if they can't tell whether you're going knee slice, long step, or smash pass, they can't defend all three simultaneously and must guess. I'll often feint one direction to get them overcommitted, then immediately switch to the now-open passing lane they've abandoned. Against high-level opponents, headquarters also gives me time to control their grips and establish my preferred grip configurations before committing to the pass, which dramatically increases my success rate in the actual passing sequence. I use headquarters especially against leg lockers because it keeps me safe from entries while I systematically break down their guard with minimal risk.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From headquarters-type positions, I'm always looking for opportunities to create unconventional control angles that traditional systematic passers tend to ignore in their focus on the standard passes. While everyone is thinking about the knee slice or long step, I'm analyzing how to use that trapped leg as an anchor point to create rotational pressure that leads into twister side control or truck position entries that open up entirely different submission systems. If the opponent is defending the standard passes effectively, they're typically not ready for you to suddenly change levels and attack their back or transition to unconventional leg positions and 10th Planet-specific controls. The 10th Planet approach is to use headquarters as a launching point for creative transitions rather than just a passing position with predetermined outcomes. For example, if they defend the knee slice by turning toward me, instead of forcing the pass through their defense I might transition to calf slicer control or even look for the truck entry if they give me their back during the defensive movement. Don't get stuck thinking headquarters only leads to side control - it can lead to much more interesting and submission-rich positions if you're willing to think outside the traditional systematic passing box. We also look for the electric chair and banana split from headquarters when the opponent tries to recover half guard, adding submission threats that create additional dilemmas beyond just the passing pressure.
